claim: Multiciliated cells (MCCs) line the epithelia of the brain ventricles, the airway, and the oviduct where motile cilia propel extracellular fluid to circulate cerebrospinal fluid, remove pathogens, and move the ova.
source: Multiciliated cells (MCCs) line the epithelia of the brain ventricles, the airway, and the oviduct where motile cilia propel extracellular fluid to circulate cerebrospinal fluid, remove pathogens, and move the ova (Spassky and Meunier, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spassky and Meunier, 2017

claim: Depending on the location, MCCs synthesize between 30 and 300 motile cilia.
source: Depending on the location, MCCs synthesize between 30 and 300 motile cilia (Spassky and Meunier, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spassky and Meunier, 2017

claim: Assembly of too few or too many cilia impairs MCC function and is associated with several diseases including Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia.
source: Assembly of too few or too many cilia impairs MCC function and is associated with several diseases including Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, suggesting the existence of an active mechanism that controls cilia number (Boon et al., 2014; Spassky and Meunier, 2017; Wallmeier et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boon et al., 2014; Spassky and Meunier, 2017; Wallmeier et al., 2014

claim: MCCs are first specified in the basal epithelia, where they begin to synthesize centrioles using specialized structures called deuterosomes.
source: There, MCCs are first specified in the basal epithelia, where they begin to synthesize centrioles using specialized structures called deuterosomes (Figure 1a, Step 0) (Klos Dehring et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klos Dehring et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1a

claim: As MCCs intercalate into the outer epithelial cell layer and expand their apical surface, centrioles migrate apically, dock at the apical surface, and provide the platform for assembly of motile cilia.
source: As MCCs intercalate into the outer epithelial cell layer and expand their apical surface, centrioles migrate apically, dock at the apical surface, and provide the platform for assembly of motile cilia (Figure 1a, Steps 1–4) (Deblandre et al., 1999; Kulkarni et al., 2018a; Stubbs et al., 2006; Zhang and Mitchell, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deblandre et al., 1999; Kulkarni et al., 2018a; Stubbs et al., 2006; Zhang and Mitchell, 2015 and reference to Figure 1a

claim: Chibby-GFP is a marker for mature centrioles.
source: As such, in this study, we focused our efforts on counting centrioles as a simple, efficient proxy for cilia number using chibby-GFP, a marker for mature centrioles (Burke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burke et al., 2014

claim: There is a strong correlation between the apical area and the number of centrioles at the apical surface in developing and mature MCCs.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a strong correlation between the apical area and the number of centrioles at the apical surface (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b,c

claim: X. laevis embryos are larger than X. tropicalis embryos.
source: First, two species of Xenopus are common models for cell biology (X. laevis and X. tropicalis), and due to the evolutionary variation in embryonic sizes of the two species, they are useful for scaling experiments (Figure 1d – compare relative sizes of the eggs and embryo) (Levy and Heald, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy and Heald, 2012 and reference to Figure 1d

claim: X. laevis MCCs have significantly larger apical areas compared to X. tropicalis MCCs (median ± SD, 391 ± 86 μm2 vs. 270 ± 53 μm2).
source: Compared to X. tropicalis, the X. laevis embryo is larger with significantly larger MCCs (Figure 1d–g, median ± SD, 391 ± 86 μm2 vs. 270 ± 53 μm2 in X. tropicalis).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1d-g with statistical measurements

claim: X. laevis MCCs have significantly more centrioles than X. tropicalis MCCs (median ± SD, 195 ± 27 compared to 150 ± 20).
source: X. laevis MCCs also have significantly more centrioles (Figure 1h, median ± SD, 195 ± 27 compared to 150 ± 20 in X. tropicalis).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1h with statistical measurements

claim: Centriole number scales with MCC apical area across X. laevis and X. tropicalis species.
source: Interestingly, by combining data from both species, we observed a clear trend where centriole number scales with MCC apical area (Figure 1i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1i

claim: Overexpression of mcidas converts epithelial goblet cells to MCCs in X. laevis.
source: Second, in X. laevis, we converted epithelial goblet cells (which normally secrete mucus) to MCCs by overexpressing the master regulator of multiciliogenesis, mcidas (multiciliate differentiation and DNA synthesis-associated cell cycle protein) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Stubbs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stubbs et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: Induced MCCs in X. laevis are larger than X. tropicalis MCCs and have proportionately more centrioles.
source: These induced MCCs in X. laevis are larger than X. tropicalis MCCs and have proportionately more centrioles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c

claim: The apical area of mature MCCs and the induced MCCs of X. laevis are similar, as are the number of centrioles.
source: Interestingly, the apical area of mature MCCs and the induced MCCs of X. laevis were similar and so were the number of centrioles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: Knocking down ccdc11 induces cytokinesis defects in X. tropicalis.
source: Third, we induced cytokinesis defects by knocking down ccdc11 using a morpholino oligo (MO) in X. tropicalis (Kulkarni et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kulkarni et al., 2018b

claim: MCCs with cytokinesis defects have significantly larger apical areas (median ± SD, 437 ± 154 μm2 vs. 202 ± 38 μm2 in controls).
source: With this strategy, we identified MCCs with significantly larger apical areas (median ± SD, 437 ± 154 μm2 vs. 202 ± 38 μm2 in controls) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b with statistical measurements

claim: MCCs with cytokinesis defects have proportionately more centrioles (median ± SD, 227 ± 74 vs. 138 ± 26 in controls).
source: and these cells had proportionately more centrioles (median ± SD, 227 ± 74 vs. 138 ± 26 in controls) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c,d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c,d with statistical measurements

claim: Fused MCCs with neighboring cells have increased apical area (median ± SD, apical area of 534 ± 149 μm2 vs. 337 ± 49 μm2 in controls).
source: Finally, in X. laevis, we fused MCCs with neighboring (most likely) non-MCCs (confirmed by the presence of two nuclei – dashed lines in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e), resulting in much larger cells with increased apical area (median ± SD, apical area of 534 ± 149 μm2 vs. 337 ± 49 μm2 in controls)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e with statistical measurements

claim: Fused MCCs have more centrioles (median ± SD, 235 ± 40 vs. 168 ± 21 in controls).
source: and more centrioles (median ± SD, 235 ± 40 vs. 168 ± 21 in controls) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–h).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e-h with statistical measurements

claim: The scaling relationship between centriole number and apical area can be observed over a 40-fold change in the apical area.
source: By combining the data from controls and manipulated embryos, we found that this scaling relationship could be observed over a 40-fold change in the apical area, with the smallest apical area being ~25 μm2 and the largest about 1000 μm2 (Figure 1j).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1j

claim: Overexpressing cep152 increases the number of centrioles in X. laevis MCCs.
source: We first increased the centriole number by overexpressing cep152 in X. laevis (Figure 2a), which increased the number of centrioles (median ± SD, 467 ± 113 vs. 160 ± 27 in controls)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a with statistical measurements and citations to Collins et al., 2020; Klos Dehring et al., 2013

claim: Overexpressing cep152 increases the apical area of MCCs (median ± SD, 692 ± 296 μm2 vs. 236 ± 58 μm2 in controls).
source: and was accompanied by a correlated increase in the apical area (median ± SD, 692 ± 296 μm2 vs. 236 ± 58 μm2 in controls) (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a-d with statistical measurements

claim: Centrinone is a PLK4 inhibitor that reduces centriole numbers.
source: Next, we reduced centriole numbers with Centrinone. Centriole synthesis begins during intercalation, when the cells are in the basal layer (Figure 1a, Step 0). To allow the chemical inhibitor to access the cells in the basal layer, we generated Xenopus embryonic 'stem cell' explants (commonly referred to as animal caps), which auto-differentiate into an embryonic epidermis replete with MCCs (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2015 and data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Centrinone treatment reduces the median number of centrioles from 104 in controls to 25 in treated MCCs.
source: We successfully reduced the median number of centrioles from 104 in controls to 25 in Centrinone-treated MCCs (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2f,g

claim: Despite a dramatic reduction in the number of centrioles, Centrinone-treated MCCs show a slight increase in apical area compared to controls (median ± SD, 175 ± 67 vs. 141 ± 38 μm2).
source: Despite a dramatic reduction in the number of centrioles, we found a slight increase in the apical area of Centrinone-treated MCCs as compared to controls (median ± SD, 175 ± 67 vs. 141 ± 38 μm2 in controls) (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2h with statistical measurements

claim: A minimum apical size can be achieved independent of centriole amplification.
source: From this result, we conclude that a minimum apical size can be achieved independent of the centriole amplification (Figure 2f–i).
evidence: Inferred from Centrinone treatment data shown in Figure 2f-i

claim: Once a minimum apical size is reached, centrioles may contribute to apical expansion.
source: Once this minimum size is reached, then centrioles may contribute to apical expansion (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: Inferred from cep152 overexpression data shown in Figure 2a-d

claim: Intercalating MCCs in X. tropicalis have a median of 75 centrioles, approximately half the number in mature MCCs.
source: In these intercalating cells, the number of centrioles was 75 (median), approximately half the number in mature X. tropicalis MCCs (Figure 3e, blue, Step 4; magenta, Steps 0–1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3e

claim: Intercalating MCCs in X. laevis have a median of 90 centrioles, approximately half the number in mature MCCs.
source: Interestingly, X. laevis MCCs also make 90 (median) centrioles during intercalation, again half the number of centrioles in mature MCCs (Figure 3f blue, Step 4; magenta, Steps 0–1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3f

claim: Xenopus MCCs synthesize half the total number of centrioles prior to intercalation.
source: From these results, we conclude that (1) Xenopus MCCs synthesize half the total number of centrioles prior to intercalation
evidence: Inferred from data on intercalating vs mature MCCs in Figure 3e,f

claim: Centrioles dock to the apical surface in a manner that scales with apical area.
source: (2) these centrioles dock to the apical surface in a manner that scales with apical area
evidence: Inferred from scaling relationship data throughout the manuscript

claim: The remaining half of the number of centrioles must be synthesized in a second round that is regulated based on the apical area.
source: and (3) the remaining half of the number of centrioles must be synthesized in a second round that is regulated based on the apical area.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that intercalating cells have half the centrioles of mature cells

claim: The thinness ratio (TR) relates the area of a shape to the square of its perimeter and can detect changes in cell shapes.
source: The thinness ratio (TR) which relates the area of a shape to the square of its perimeter can detect these changes in cell shapes (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on established mathematical definition shown in Figure 4a

claim: The TR is 1 for a circle and < 1 for polygons.
source: The TR is 1 for a circle and < 1 for polygons (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on mathematical definition shown in Figure 4a

claim: MCCs with small apical areas have a TR of nearly 1, while the TR decreases to 0.8 as the apical area increases to ~300 μm2.
source: When we plotted the TR as a function of apical area, we found that MCCs with small apical areas have a TR of nearly 1, while the TR decreases to 0.8 as the apical area increases to ~300 μm2 (Figure 4b,c, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c and Video 3

claim: Initial apical expansion is driven by cell autonomous pushing forces, while subsequent apical expansion is driven largely by cell non-autonomous pulling forces.
source: Therefore, TR measurements support the notion that the initial apical expansion is driven by cell autonomous pushing forces, while subsequent apical expansion is driven largely by cell non-autonomous pulling forces.
evidence: Inferred from TR measurements and cell shape analysis in Figure 4b,c

claim: β-catenin-depleted embryos lack dorsal structures and have much less elongation compared to control embryos.
source: By depleting β-catenin, a key effector of the Wnt signaling pathway, we can eliminate the formation of Spemann's Organizer and generate cylindrically symmetric embryos that lack dorsal structures and have much less elongation compared to control embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c, Heasman et al., 1994; Khokha et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heasman et al., 1994; Khokha et al., 2005 and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c

claim: β-catenin-depleted embryos can form functioning MCCs that generate fluid flow.
source: While β-catenin-depleted embryos can form functioning MCCs that generate fluid flow, both the MCCs (median ± SD, 106 ± 26 μm2 vs. 267 ± 64 μm2 in controls) and non-MCCs (median ± SD, 319 ± 104 μm2 vs. 428 ± 125 μm2 in controls,) have smaller apical areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,d–f).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,d-f with statistical measurements

claim: β-catenin-depleted MCCs have significantly decreased centriole number (median ± SD, 100 ± 16 vs. 148 ± 26 in controls).
source: Interestingly, the centriole number in these embryos is also significantly decreased (median ± SD, 100 ± 16 vs. 148 ± 26 in controls, Figure 4—figure supplement 1g,h), approaching the 75 centrioles formed prior to intercalation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g,h with statistical measurements

claim: The TR in β-catenin-depleted MCCs is significantly higher and closer to 1 (median ± SD, 0.93 ± 0.05 vs. 0.77 ± 0.04 in controls).
source: Further, the TR in β-catenin-depleted MCCs is significantly higher and closer to 1 (median ± SD, 0.93 ± 0.05 vs. 0.77 ± 0.04 in controls, Figure 4—figure supplement 1i,j), supportive of a significant reduction of pulling forces exerted on MCCs.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i,j with statistical measurements

claim: MCCs in untethered animal caps have an apical area just slightly larger than in β-catenin-depleted embryos (median ± SD, 116 ± 37 μm2 compared to 106 ± 26 μm2 in β-catenin-depleted embryos and 263 ± 46 μm2 in controls).
source: The MCCs in these explants had an apical area just slightly larger than in β-catenin-depleted embryos (median ± SD, 116 ± 37 μm2 compared to 106 ± 26 μm2 in β-catenin-depleted embryos and 263 ± 46 μm2 in controls, Figure 4e,f,i)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4e,f,i with statistical measurements

claim: MCCs in untethered animal caps have a correlated decrease in centriole number (median ± SD, 105 ± 27 compared to 100 ± 16 in β-catenin-depleted embryos and 149 ± 14 in controls).
source: and a correlated decrease in centriole number (median ± SD, 105 ± 27 compared to 100 ± 16 in β-catenin-depleted embryos and 149 ± 14 in controls, Figure 4j).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4j with statistical measurements

claim: MCCs in tethered animal caps have increased apical area (median ± SD, 210 ± 43 μm2 compared to 116 ± 37 μm2 in untethered caps compared to 263 ± 46 μm2 in controls).
source: In these tethered explants, the apical area of both non-MCCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, median ± SD, 372 ± 159 μm2 compared to 170 ± 86 μm2 in untethered caps and 465 ± 177 μm2 in controls) and the MCCs (Figure 4e–g,i, median ± SD, 210 ± 43 μm2 compared to 116 ± 37 μm2 in untethered caps compared to 263 ± 46 μm2 in controls) are increased compared to the untethered caps
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4e-g,i with statistical measurements

claim: Tethered animal caps have a significant increase in the number of centrioles (median ± SD, 130 ± 25 vs 105 ± 27 in untethered caps compared to 149 ± 14 in controls) in an area-dependent manner.
source: Nevertheless, the tethered caps had a significant increase in the number of centrioles (Figure 4j, median ± SD, 130 ± 25 vs 105 ± 27 in untethered caps compared to 149 ± 14 in controls) in an area-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4j with statistical measurements

claim: Mechanical stretching of animal caps creates a force of 11.5 N and about 50–75% strain.
source: At this stage, MCCs are nearly mature, and we stretched the explants radially for 3 hr in a stepwise fashion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2e,f). This stepwise stretch created a force of 11.5 N and about 50–75% strain.
evidence: Supported by experimental design shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2e,f

claim: Mechanical stretching leads to a significant increase in the apical area of MCCs (median ± SD, 409 ± 57 μm2 compared to 210 ± 43 μm2 in unstretched tethered caps).
source: We observed a significant increase in the apical area of MCCs (median ± SD, 409 ± 57 μm2 compared to 210 ± 43 μm2 in unstretched tethered caps) (Figure 4g–i).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4g-i with statistical measurements

claim: Stretching leads to a dramatic change in cell shape and a further significant reduction in the TR (apical area: 351–600 μm2, median ± SD, TR: 0.71 ± 0.1) compared to both tethered unstretched caps (median ± SD, TR: 0.79 ± 0.6) and WT X. tropicalis MCCs (median ± SD, TR: 0.79 ± 0.6).
source: Stretching also led to a dramatic change in cell shape and a further significant reduction in the TR (apical area: 351–600 μm2, median ± SD, TR: 0.71 ± 0.1, Figure 4c,d) compared to both tethered unstretched caps (median ± SD, TR: 0.79 ± 0.6) and WT X. tropicalis MCCs (median ± SD, TR: 0.79 ± 0.6)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4c,d with statistical measurements

claim: In stretched MCCs, the number of centrioles increases (median ± SD, 199 ± 33 vs 130 ± 25 in unstretched tethered caps).
source: In these stretched MCCs, the number of centrioles also increased (median ± SD, 199 ± 33 vs 130 ± 25 in unstretched tethered caps) demonstrating that stretching forces trigger centriole amplification in an area dependent manner in MCCs (Figure 4j).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4j with statistical measurements

claim: Stretching transforms MCCs in X. tropicalis explants to sizes similar to X. laevis (median ± SD, 409 ± 57 μm2 vs. 390 ± 87 μm2 in X. laevis) with similar centriole numbers (median ± SD, 199 ± 33 vs. 195 ± 27 in X. laevis).
source: Interestingly, just by stretching, we transformed MCCs in X. tropicalis explants to sizes more similar to X. laevis (median ± SD, 409 ± 57 μm2 vs. 390 ± 87 μm2 in X. laevis) and the number of centrioles generated were also similar (median ± SD, 199 ± 33 vs. 195 ± 27 in X. laevis), highlighting the conserved role of mechanical forces in establishing the scaling mechanisms across species (Figure 1g–j, Figure 4k).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1g-j and Figure 4k with statistical measurements

claim: Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that responds directly to membrane stretch and is primarily expressed in epithelial cells exposed to fluid pressure and flow.
source: Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that responds directly to membrane stretch and is primarily expressed in epithelial cells exposed to fluid pressure and flow (Bagriantsev et al., 2014; Wang and Xiao, 2018; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bagriantsev et al., 2014; Wang and Xiao, 2018; Wu et al., 2017

claim: Piezo1 is localized adjacent to the centrioles at the apical membrane.
source: In addition to its expression at cell junctions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b – dashed box), we unexpectedly discovered that Piezo1 is localized adjacent to the centrioles at the apical membrane (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b

claim: Piezo1 localization is diminished with MO-based Piezo1 depletion.
source: Piezo1 localization is diminished with MO-based Piezo1 depletion indicating that this anti-Piezo1 antibody signal is specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c-e

claim: Depletion of Piezo1 using MO, CRISPR, or inhibition with GSMTx4 results in a significant decrease in centriole number compared to control embryos (median ± SD, 105 ± 22 piezo1 MO, 116 ± 24 piezo1 CRISPR, and 110 ± 26 GSMTx4, compared to 140 ± 21 in uninjected controls and 133 ± 22 in standard MO controls).
source: Centrioles were measured in mature MCCs and all three treatments resulted in a significant decrease in centriole number compared to control embryos (Figure 5b,d–g, median ± SD, 105 ± 22 piezo1 MO, 116 ± 24 piezo1 CRISPR, and 110 ± 26 GSMTx4, compared to 140 ± 21 in uninjected controls and 133 ± 22 in standard MO controls).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5b,d-g with statistical measurements

claim: Piezo1 depletion uncouples the relationship between apical area and centriole number.
source: Further, Piezo1 depletion also uncoupled the relationship between apical area and centriole number as evident by the increase instead of a decrease in the apical area (Figure 5c–g) and flattening of the regression line in the treated embryos (Figure 5h–k).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5c-g and Figure 5h-k

claim: Piezo1 is essential for calibrating centriole number in relation to the apical area in MCCs.
source: Our results demonstrate that Piezo1 is essential for calibrating centriole number in relation to the apical area in MCCs.
evidence: Inferred from all Piezo1 manipulation experiments shown in Figure 5

claim: Piezo1 is not essential to generate the first 100 centrioles but calibrates the final 50 centrioles in response to pulling forces.
source: Thus, our data suggest that Piezo1 is not essential to generate the first 100 centrioles but calibrates the final 50 centrioles in response to pulling forces.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Piezo1-depleted embryos with β-catenin depleted MCCs and untethered animal caps

claim: In untethered animal caps, centriole number does not significantly differ between controls and Piezo1 depleted MCCs (median ± SD, 101 ± 15 vs. 94 ± 15).
source: In the context of untethered animal caps, centriole number did not significantly differ in controls and Piezo1 depleted MCCs (Figure 6a,c, median ± SD, 101 ± 15 vs. 94 ± 15).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6a,c with statistical measurements

claim: In tethered animal caps, Piezo1 depletion leads to a significant reduction in centriole number compared to controls (median ± SD, 119 ± 14 in controls vs. 109 ± 16).
source: In contrast, in tethered animal caps, Piezo one depletion led to a significant reduction in centriole number compared to controls (Figure 6b,d, median ± SD, 119 ± 14 in controls vs. 109 ± 16).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6b,d with statistical measurements

claim: With Piezo1 depletion, the number of centrioles in MCCs of tethered caps is similar to wild-type MCCs of untethered caps (median 109 in Piezo1 depleted compared to 101 in controls).
source: Interestingly, with Piezo1 depletion, the number of centrioles in MCCs of tethered caps was similar to wild-type MCCs of untethered caps (median 109 in Piezo1 depleted compared to 101 in controls), demonstrating that Piezo1 is required for stretch-induced centriole amplification in the MCCs of Xenopus.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6

claim: Piezo1 is required for stretch-induced centriole amplification in the MCCs of Xenopus.
source: demonstrating that Piezo1 is required for stretch-induced centriole amplification in the MCCs of Xenopus.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6

claim: The stretching of MCCs due to morphogenetic movements calibrates centriole number in proportion to the apical area via Piezo1.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrated that the stretching of MCCs due to morphogenetic movements calibrates centriole number in proportion to the apical area via Piezo1.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data on stretching and Piezo1 manipulation

claim: A previous study using mouse tracheal epithelial cell culture suggested a correlation between cilia number and the apical area.
source: While a previous study using mouse tracheal epithelial cell culture suggested a correlation between cilia number and the apical area (Nanjundappa et al., 2019), the underlying mechanism was unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nanjundappa et al., 2019

claim: Centriole amplification occurs while the MCCs are being stretched and expanding their apical surface.
source: Importantly, centriole amplification occurs while the MCCs are being stretched and expanding their apical surface.
evidence: Inferred from developmental timing data shown in Figure 1a and throughout the manuscript

claim: Piezo1 translates the pulling forces that define the apical area into an appropriate number of centrioles.
source: Our results show that Piezo1 translates the pulling forces that define the apical area into an appropriate number of centrioles (Figure 6f).
evidence: Inferred from all Piezo1 and mechanical force experiments, summarized in Figure 6f

claim: Piezo1-mediated mechanosensation couples apical area and centriole number.
source: Thus, Piezo1-mediated mechanosensation couples apical area and centriole number (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data, summarized in Figure 6e,f

claim: Stretch may activate Piezo1, which leads to an influx of Ca2+ from the extracellular environment, potentially promoting centriole amplification via transcriptional or non-transcriptional means.
source: One possibility is that stretch may activate Piezo1, which leads to an influx of Ca2+ from the extracellular environment. This increase in intracellular Ca2+ may promote centriole amplification via either transcriptional or non-transcriptional means.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on known Piezo1 function

claim: Piezo1 has been shown to regulate the expression of focal adhesion kinases (FAK, Paxillin and Vinculin) in cancer cells leading to changes in tissue stiffness.
source: Alternatively, Piezo1 has been shown to regulate the expression of focal adhesion kinases (FAK, Paxillin and Vinculin) in cancer cells leading to changes in tissue stiffness (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018

claim: Focal adhesion kinases (FAK, Paxillin and Vinculin) localize to the bases of cilia in MCCs, and their downregulation causes defects in actin and cilia assembly.
source: These three focal adhesion kinases localize to the bases of cilia in MCCs, and their downregulation causes defects in actin and cilia assembly (Antoniades et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Antoniades et al., 2014

claim: Filamentous (F)-actin plays a critical role in mechanotransduction in all cells.
source: Finally, filamentous (F)-actin plays a critical role in mechanotransduction in all cells (Massou et al., 2020; Wang, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Massou et al., 2020; Wang, 2017

claim: MCCs are enriched in F-actin at the apical membrane.
source: At the apical membrane, MCCs are enriched in F-actin
evidence: Observed in multiple figures showing phalloidin staining

claim: The apparent loss of apical F-actin in Piezo1-depleted cells may lead to defective mechanotransduction resulting in defects in centriole amplification and apical area.
source: and the apparent loss of apical F-actin in Piezo1-depleted cells may lead to defective mechanotransduction resulting in the defects in centriole amplification and apical area.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on observations

claim: Mammalian MCCs do not radially intercalate like Xenopus MCCs, but they still scale centriole number to the apical area suggesting a conserved mechanism.
source: While mammalian MCCs do not radially intercalate like Xenopus MCCs, they still scale centriole number to the apical area suggesting a conserved mechanism (Nanjundappa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nanjundappa et al., 2019

claim: The formation of MCCs in the mammalian respiratory epithelium is similar to the goblet cells converted to MCCs by mcidas overexpression in Xenopus.
source: Indeed, the formation of MCCs in the mammalian respiratory epithelium is similar to the goblet cells converted to MCCs by mcidas overexpression in Xenopus, which also scale centriole number to the apical area.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mammalian MCCs and mcidas overexpression data

claim: Mechanical stretch scales centriole number to apical area via Piezo1 in multiciliated cells.
source: Mechanical stretch scales centriole number to apical area via Piezo1 in multiciliated cells
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data
